passage: I'm Sudha. Last Saturday I went to Hemant's house for his birthday. At the door his mother asked if I had eggs in my tiffin, because their kitchen has no eggs at all. Inside I saw two sets of steel plates, and Hemant's Dadi ate only from her own. I wanted to giggle, because at our house Papa makes egg curry every Sunday. But I remembered how Anjali laughed at my fish smell last year and how bad it felt. So I asked Hemant, 'Why two sets?' He said, 'Dadi's are for her fasting days.' I said, 'Oh. We have a special plate for Nani too.' He looked relieved.

qa.q: Why does Hemant's Dadi have her own plates?
qa.a: Dadi's are for her fasting days.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling on wanting to giggle, and what stopped it?
qa.a: Sudha felt amused and curious, but remembered how hurt and embarrassed Anjali's laughing at the fish smell had made Sudha feel.

qa.q: What could another child learn from how Sudha asked about the plates?
qa.a: To ask kindly and share something similar from home instead of laughing, which keeps the friendship easy.

qa.q: How did Hemant seem to feel when Sudha asked kindly?
qa.a: Hemant seemed relieved, perhaps because he expected teasing and was met with interest instead.

grounding: Shows a child noticing a friend's home has different kitchen rules, such as no eggs and separate plates, and choosing to ask kindly rather than mock.

passage:
Thursday: At Ojas's house for a school project, Kashish, nine, notices a small shelf of blue plates kept apart from the steel ones. Ojas's Aai serves Kashish on steel. Why blue? Kashish wonders, but says nothing.
Saturday: Kashish asks Ma at home. Ma says, 'Why not ask Ojas? Kindly, like you're curious, not like it's weird.'
Monday: At recess Kashish asks, 'Ojas, what are the blue plates for?' Ojas shrugs. 'For chicken. Aaji doesn't eat it, so we keep hers separate.' Kashish nods. 'We don't eat onion in Navratri, so Ma keeps a separate pan too.' Ojas grins. 'Everyone has a weird pan.'

qa.q: What are the blue plates for?
qa.a: For chicken.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling on Thursday on seeing the blue plates?
qa.a: Kashish felt curious and a little unsure, wondering about the plates but too shy to ask right away.

qa.q: Which part of Ma's advice made the Monday talk go well?
qa.a: Asking out of curiosity, not as if the custom were strange, so Ojas could explain without feeling mocked.

qa.q: How does Ojas seem to feel about explaining the blue plates?
qa.a: Ojas seems relaxed and at ease, even joking that everyone has a weird pan, because Kashish asked kindly.

grounding: Illustrates a child who notices a friend's home keeps separate plates, and learns to ask kindly out of curiosity rather than mock, keeping the friendship open.

passage:
Abhinav, you laughed at Rishabh's tiffin today because it had no onion? Come here. Let your Gargi Nani tell you about Mitali.

When I was nine in Kolkata, I went to my friend Mitali's house for the first time. In our Jain home there were no eggs, no onions, nothing from under the ground. In her kitchen, a whole fish lay on the chopping board, eyes and all.

I said, "Chhi! You eat that?"

Mitali's face fell. Her mother came in and didn't scold me. She said, "Your house cooks one way, ours another. Would you like to help me make luchi?"

I stood beside her and asked a hundred questions, kindly this time.

Mitali and I stayed friends for sixty years. That "Chhi" is the one word I would take back.

qa.q: What lay on the chopping board in Mitali's kitchen?
qa.a: A whole fish lay on the chopping board, eyes and all.

qa.q: How does Gargi feel now about her 'Chhi'?
qa.a: Gargi deeply regrets it; it is the one word she would take back, because it hurt Mitali.

qa.q: What turning point changed how young Gargi reacted to Mitali's kitchen?
qa.a: Mitali's mother calmly explained that each house cooks its own way and invited her to help with luchi, so kind questions replaced mocking.

qa.q: How did Mitali feel when Gargi said 'Chhi'?
qa.a: Mitali felt hurt and embarrassed; her face fell at the insult to her family's food.

grounding: Shows a child noticing a friend's home has different kitchen rules, mocking at first, and learning that asking kindly keeps the friendship open.

passage:
The rain was so heavy that Jyoti's father rang to say he couldn't fetch her till nine, so Jyoti, ten, stayed for dinner at Farida's.

The whole flat smelled of chicken biryani. Jyoti's stomach twisted; at home, not even eggs came through the door.

But Farida's Ammi set a separate plate in front of her. "Dal-khichdi, made in the new steel pot. Nothing else has touched it."

Jyoti stared. "You have a special pot?"

"For Farida's vegetarian friends," Ammi smiled. "You're the third."

Farida leaned over. "At your house, why do you have two sets of spoons?"

"One for Paryushan days," Jyoti said, then paused. "Actually, I'm not sure why. I'll ask Mummy."

"Tell me tomorrow," said Farida, and passed her the pickle.

qa.q: What did Farida's Ammi make for Jyoti?
qa.a: Dal-khichdi, made in the new steel pot.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she smelled the chicken biryani?
qa.a: Jyoti felt uneasy, her stomach twisting, because at home not even eggs came through the door.

qa.q: What kept the evening friendly despite the different kitchen rules?
qa.a: Ammi quietly made separate food, and both girls asked each other questions kindly instead of mocking.

qa.q: How might Farida see Jyoti's family's rules?
qa.a: Farida is curious rather than dismissive, asking about the two sets of spoons and wanting to hear the answer tomorrow.

grounding: Shows a child noticing that a friend's home has different food and utensil rules, with kind curiosity on both sides keeping the friendship open.

passage:
At Mahima's flat in Lajpat Nagar, Sunday breakfast was omelettes, a whole stack, yellow and puffy. Vandana, nine, had never seen an egg on a plate at home.

The word "eww" was already in her mouth. Then she remembered Kunal laughing at her aloo paratha tiffin last week, and how hot her face had gone.

She swallowed the word. "What does it taste like?"

"Like egg," Mahima giggled. "Mummy puts onion and chilli. Want to try?"

"We don't eat eggs," Vandana said. "But can I watch her make it?"

Mahima's mother let her crack one into the bowl. Vandana squealed at the slimy feel and washed her hands three times, laughing.

She ate toast and jam. Mahima ate two omelettes. Nobody said eww.

qa.q: What was Sunday breakfast at Mahima's flat?
qa.a: Sunday breakfast was omelettes, a whole stack.

qa.q: Why did Vandana swallow the word 'eww'?
qa.a: She remembered how embarrassed and hurt she had felt when Kunal laughed at her tiffin, and didn't want Mahima to feel that.

qa.q: What could Vandana tell a classmate who mocks someone's food?
qa.a: That asking what it tastes like, as she did, keeps things friendly, and that everyone's home food matters to them.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel when Vandana asks what the omelette tastes like?
qa.a: Mahima feels comfortable and pleased, happily explaining and inviting Vandana to try.

grounding: Shows a child noticing a friend's home eats eggs when hers does not, and choosing kind curiosity over mocking.

passage:
"Kavitha, why do you have two sets of plates?"
"Those are for Ammamma. She doesn't eat from plates that had eggs."
Anjali looked around the kitchen. "No eggs at all?"
"Not in this kitchen. Appa eats omelettes at the canteen."
"At my house we have eggs every morning. And fish on Sundays."
"Really? Fish?" Kavitha wrinkled her nose, then laughed. "Sorry. Is it nice?"
"Very nice. Is Ammamma angry if I bring my egg sandwich?"
"Hmm. Maybe eat it on the balcony? Then it's not in the kitchen."
"Okay." Anjali thought. "Can I try your Ammamma's sambar?"
Kavitha's grandmother, listening from the door, smiled and filled a small bowl. "Ask me anything, kanna. Better than guessing."
Anjali tasted it. "Can you teach my mum?"

qa.q: Why does Kavitha's house have two sets of plates?
qa.a: Because Ammamma doesn't eat from plates that had eggs.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling as she looked around the kitchen?
qa.a: Anjali felt curious and a little surprised, noticing rules very different from her own home.

qa.q: How did Anjali and Kavitha keep the friendship open?
qa.a: They asked each other kindly about eggs and fish instead of mocking, and found an easy solution like eating on the balcony.

qa.q: How might Kavitha's grandmother feel about Anjali's questions?
qa.a: She seems pleased and warm, smiling and inviting Anjali to ask rather than guess.

grounding: It illustrates a child noticing a friend's home has different kitchen rules and asking kindly rather than mocking.
